p.src: A Plane Wave Along the $z$-Axis

u.src: A Plane Wave Along the $z$-Axis
en: A Plane Wave Along the $z$-Axis

p.src:
Choose coordinates so that the wave propagates along the $z$-axis. This costs no generality; a wave in another direction can be brought to this form by rotating the axes. Let $k$ be its wave number, $\lambda=\frac{2\pi}{k},$ and let $\omega$ be its frequency. Before imposing any equation of motion, write all six field components with a common phase $\theta=kz-\omega t:$ $\begin{aligned}
E_x(z,t)&=\epsilon_x\sin\theta,
&
B_x(z,t)&=\beta_x\sin\theta,
\nonumber\\
E_y(z,t)&=\epsilon_y\sin\theta,
&
B_y(z,t)&=\beta_y\sin\theta,
\\
E_z(z,t)&=\epsilon_z\sin\theta,
&
B_z(z,t)&=\beta_z\sin\theta.
\nonumber\end{aligned}$ The six Greek letters are constant amplitudes.

p.src: Why begin with the same sinusoidal dependence for $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$? Suppose one field carried $\sin\theta$ and the other carried $\cos\theta$. A time derivative on one side of a curl equation and a spatial derivative on the other would then produce different trigonometric functions. The equality could not hold for every $z$ and $t$. A common constant phase is allowed, but translating the origin of $z$ removes it. Thus the ansatz is not an extra dynamical law; it is the simplest representative of the phase relation the differential equations will require.

p.src:
Because the fields depend only on $z$ and $t$, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf E
=
\partial_xE_x+\partial_yE_y+\partial_zE_z
=
\partial_zE_z.$ In empty space this must vanish for every phase, so $\epsilon_z=0.$ The identical argument for the magnetic field gives $\beta_z=0.$ Neither field has a component along the direction of propagation. The wave is transverse.

p.src:
Use the $x$-component of $\dot{\mathbf E}=-\nabla\times\mathbf B$. Since the fields vary only with $z$, $\dot E_x
=
-\left(\nabla\times\mathbf B\right)_x
=
\partial_zB_y.$ Substituting the ansatz gives $\begin{aligned}
-\omega\epsilon_x\cos\theta
&=
k\beta_y\cos\theta,
\nonumber\\
\beta_y
&=
-\,\epsilon_x\frac{\omega}{k}.
\end{aligned}$ The $y$-component of the same Maxwell equation reads $\dot E_y
=
-\left(\partial_zB_x\right).$ The left side is zero by our polarization choice, so $\beta_x=0.$

p.src:
Combining equations  and  gives the dispersion relation $\left(\frac{\omega}{k}\right)^2=1.$ For the positive-frequency wave moving in the chosen direction, $\omega=k
\qquad
(c=1).$ The common phase is consequently $\theta=k(z-t).$ Restoring ordinary units gives $\omega=ck,
\qquad
\theta=k(z-ct).$ Thus the profile moves rigidly at the speed of light. In the units used on the board, the electric and magnetic amplitudes have equal magnitude. Their relative minus sign is an orientation convention: it says which way the chosen $y$-axis points, not that one field lags the other by a quarter cycle.

p.src: Maxwell’s equations are linear. The amplitude $\epsilon_x$ may be large or small, $\beta_y$ follows from it, and any sum or difference of solutions is again a solution. Waves traveling in different directions may therefore be superposed. This brief calculation is worth doing: an account of electromagnetism should not leave the electromagnetic wave as an unexplained quotation.

p.src: We now turn from a particular solution to the structure of the theory. The principle of least action is what organizes energy conservation, momentum conservation, and their relation to spacetime symmetries. One can invent differential equations that possess no energy worth calling conserved and no useful symmetry principle. Maxwell’s equations should instead arise from a Lagrangian.

p.src:
The first principle is locality. An action is an integral over spacetime of a density built from fields and their first derivatives at the same point: $S=\int d^4x\,\mathcal L(\phi,\phi_{,\mu}),
\qquad
\phi_{,\mu}\equiv\partial_\mu\phi.$ The comma is a compact derivative notation. The second principle is Lorentz invariance: $\mathcal L$ must be a scalar.

p.src:
Before varying a four-vector, rehearse the method with one scalar field. A local Lorentz scalar may depend on a potential $U(\phi)$ and on the contraction of two derivatives: $\mathcal L_\phi
=
-\frac12\,\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi-U(\phi).$ With the mostly-plus metric, $\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi
=
-\dot\phi^{\,2}+|\nabla\phi|^2,$ so $\mathcal L_\phi
=
\frac12\dot\phi^{\,2}
-\frac12|\nabla\phi|^2
-U(\phi).$ The raised time derivative differs in sign from the lowered one; raised and lowered spatial derivatives do not.

p.src:
The field Euler–Lagrange equation is $\partial_\mu\left(
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\phi_{,\mu}}
\right)
=
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\phi}.$ For , $\frac{\partial\mathcal L_\phi}{\partial\phi_{,\mu}}
=
-\partial^\mu\phi,
\qquad
\frac{\partial\mathcal L_\phi}{\partial\phi}
=
-U'(\phi),$ and hence $\Box\phi=U'(\phi),
\qquad
\Box\equiv\partial_\mu\partial^\mu.$ Equivalently, $\ddot\phi-\nabla^2\phi=-U'(\phi).$ On the board only the $x$-derivative is written before the $y$ and $z$ terms are left implicit. The result is the familiar wave equation with a force from the potential.

p.src:
Select the derivative $A_{x,y}=\partial_yA_x$. The $xy$ and $yx$ terms in the full sum contribute $\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{EM}}
&\supset
-\frac14\left(F_{xy}F^{xy}+F_{yx}F^{yx}\right)
\nonumber\\
&=
-\frac12F_{xy}^2
\nonumber\\
&=
-\frac12\left(A_{x,y}-A_{y,x}\right)^2.
\end{aligned}$ The last equality is safe because the sign disappears upon squaring: $A_{x,y}-A_{y,x}=F_{yx}=-F_{xy}$.

p.src:
The same conclusion follows more cleanly by varying the whole action: $\begin{aligned}
\delta S_{\mathrm{EM}}
&=
-\frac12\int d^4x\,
F^{\mu\nu}
\left(\partial_\mu\delta A_\nu
-\partial_\nu\delta A_\mu\right)
\nonumber\\
&=
-\int d^4x\,F^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\delta A_\nu
\nonumber\\
&=
\int d^4x\,
\left(\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}\right)\delta A_\nu,
\end{aligned}$ where the boundary term is discarded. Antisymmetry combines the two terms in the first line. Since $\delta A_\nu$ is arbitrary,  follows.

p.src: The Conserved Four-Current

u.src: The Conserved Four-Current
en: The Conserved Four-Current

p.src:
The source is the four-current $J^\mu=(\rho,\mathbf J).$ Its time component is charge density and its spatial components are the charge fluxes through three mutually perpendicular windows. Equivalently, for a small fixed box, $\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}
+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0.$ Charge inside the box can decrease only by flowing through its boundary. In covariant notation, $\boxed{\partial_\mu J^\mu=0.}$

p.src:
To see the mechanism in elementary terms, expand the contraction: $J^\mu\partial_\mu\chi
=
J^0\partial_0\chi
+J^1\partial_1\chi
+J^2\partial_2\chi
+J^3\partial_3\chi.$ Assume the current is confined to a large laboratory or falls off fast enough that it vanishes at the boundary. Integrate each term by parts. For the first spatial coordinate, for example, $\begin{aligned}
-\int d^4x\,J^1\partial_1\chi
&=
-\int dt\,dx^2\,dx^3
\left[J^1\chi\right]_{x^1=-\infty}^{x^1=+\infty}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+\int d^4x\,\chi\,\partial_1J^1
\nonumber\\
&=
\int d^4x\,\chi\,\partial_1J^1.\end{aligned}$ The same operation applies to the time term and the other two spatial terms.

p.src: If one asks for the most economical constructive route, the combination of locality, Lorentz invariance, gauge invariance, and a Lagrangian principle selects $-\frac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}-J^\mu A_\mu$ and hence Maxwell’s dynamical equation. Calling one entry in this triangle more fundamental is partly a matter of taste. The important fact is that the entries fit.

p.src: This is a large amount of structure: Lagrangian mechanics, relativistic field theory, electrodynamics, Lorentz invariance, gauge invariance, and local charge conservation have become parts of one argument. The only reliable way to digest it is to start again with the equations and carry each derivative and sign through by hand.
